name: Wei Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you tell me stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a curtain-sider for a builders' merchant, so timber, plasterboard, bags of cement, roof tiles, out to building sites. It's got a loader crane on the back, a little hydraulic arm I work with a remote, so I lift the packs off myself. The best part is a tidy drop where the site manager's ready and I can swing a pack of tiles onto a scaffold in one go. The worst part is a muddy site with no space, a skip in the way and a foreman shouting at me to hurry.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up doing this, and what's home life like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I started in the yard at nineteen, loading, then the firm paid for my licence and the crane ticket. I live with my girlfriend Ana, who's a nurse on a children's ward, in a rented two-bed near the industrial estate. I'll use a chatbot now and then, to check a rule about weights or help write a complaint to the council about a pothole, but I'm not glued to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype people got it wrong again. Probably a meme in the group chat with the lads from the yard, something about the robot that couldn't find the site entrance. Then back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved. Building keeps going in any picture where nothing changes, and somebody has to get the plasterboard up to the third floor. The only thing on my mind would be that rents keep climbing and Ana and I want our own place one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, maybe ask the boss about the bigger crane ticket so I can work the long-reach trucks, which pay a bit more. I'd keep putting money into the deposit pot, about two hundred a month. I'd still use the chatbot for small stuff, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a boring answer, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a slow month on the building sites do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter we had two weeks of rain and half the sites stopped ordering. I still got my basic pay, but no overtime, so maybe three hundred less that month. We dipped into savings for the car insurance, which annoyed me more than it should have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the union matter to you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'm in it, I pay the dues. In a normal picture it's mostly about pay talks and making sure nobody gets sent out with a crane that's not been inspected. It's like insurance, you hope you never need it.

say: I'd tell the yard group chat the **hype was wrong** again.
I'd joke about the robot that couldn't **find the site entrance**.
think: **Building work** carries on, so the job feels safe.
The real worry is **rent** and getting our own place.
do: Ask the boss about the **long-reach crane** ticket for better pay.
Keep putting about **two hundred a month** into the house deposit pot.
feel: **Calm**, in a plain and unexciting way.
S0.quote: Building keeps going in any picture where nothing changes, and somebody has to get the plasterboard up to the third floor.
fieldNote: His crane skill makes him feel **useful on site** in ways a van driver isn't.
**Wet winters** cutting overtime are his main existing money worry.
He sees the union as **insurance** rather than a cause.

steps.text: Ask the builders' merchant to fund the long-reach crane ticket
Keep two hundred a month going into the house deposit
Keep delivering to building sites on the same routes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe the paperwork side gets easier, but the bosses shouldn't use it as an excuse to cut people. I'd share union stuff online about protecting jobs in the office, because those are people I know. I'd say the crane still needs a person on the remote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the yard office shrinks first. The girl who takes orders over the phone, the bloke who plans the routes, both could be a program in this picture. My job's safer for now, but the schedule gets tighter because a computer thinks I can do six drops when four is honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new ordering and routing app properly, because if they bring it in I want to know how it works so I can argue with it. I'd go to the union meetings about it. And I'd keep the deposit savings going but maybe hold off on the new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, for the office lot, and a bit for what my days turn into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you argue with the app about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Site access, mainly. The routing app sees a postcode. The app doesn't see that the gate's round the back and a cement mixer blocks it till ten. If I can show the planner that with the app's own data, I've got a case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hold off on the new car. Why that, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the one big thing we'd been planning on credit, and in a picture where things are shifting I don't want a monthly payment I can't drop. The old car's fine, it just rattles. Ana says it sounds like a tin of nails.

say: I'd say bosses shouldn't use AI as an **excuse to cut** people.
I'd point out the **crane** still needs a person on the remote.
think: The **yard office** shrinks first, with ordering and planning done by software.
My days get **tighter schedules** from a computer that doesn't know sites.
do: Learn the **routing app** properly so he can challenge it with data.
Go to **union meetings** about the new systems.
Hold off on the **new car** loan while things shift.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for the office staff and partly for his own days.
S1.quote: The routing app sees a postcode. The app doesn't see that the gate's round the back and a cement mixer blocks it till ten.
fieldNote: He would **learn the tool** to fight it, which fits a steady, practical person.
His sympathy goes to **office colleagues** before himself.
Cancelling the **car loan** shows real caution under the calm surface.

steps.text: Learn the new routing app well enough to challenge drop counts
Attend union meetings on the yard's new ordering software
Put off buying a new car on credit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loud and clear that the government needs a plan for millions of drivers, not a press release. I'd be sharing stuff about a transition fund, and I'd probably go to a rally. I'd tell the yard lads to get organised now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, in two years the yard office is gone and the orders come from an AI. Then by 2031 there's a robot truck that can probably work its own crane. I'd be thirty-one, and the bit of my job I'm proud of, the tricky drops, is exactly what they'll train the robots on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd look at what's left hands-on that robots will struggle with longest, maybe scaffolding or site work, where nothing's ever in the same place twice. I'd talk to Ana about moving the house plan back. I'd cut the takeaways and the football season ticket, and save harder for the three years before the robots land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight chest kind of feeling, but I'd be doing something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three years between the thinking AI and the robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to get paid while I look, mainly. The driving lasts three years longer than the office, so I'd keep driving and use my days off to try site work, maybe shadow a scaffolder I know. It's not much of a head start, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ana's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I reckon nursing on a kids' ward is one of the last things people will hand to a robot. Parents want a person. We'd be leaning on my girlfriend's wage, which is weird for me, because I always thought I'd be the steady one.

say: I'd say the government needs a **real plan** for millions of drivers.
I'd go to a **rally** and tell the yard lads to organise.
think: The **yard office** goes in two years and robots follow by 2031.
The **tricky drops** I'm proud of are what robots will learn from.
do: Try **scaffolding or site work** on days off while still driving.
Cut **takeaways** and the football season ticket to save harder.
Move the **house plan** back with Ana.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest, but busy doing something about it.
S2.quote: Nursing on a kids' ward is one of the last things people will hand to a robot. Parents want a person.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the driving job** but still feels some control.
His partner's **nursing job** is the household's safety net.
He uses the **three-year gap** as paid time to test site work.

steps.text: Shadow a scaffolder on days off to test site work
Drop the football season ticket and weekly takeaways
Push back the plan to buy a house with Ana
Go to rallies calling for a transition fund for drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, get the union and the government building a proper training scheme. I'd share that kind of thing online. Less shouting than the fast one, more organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it still finishes the driving for me, just at thirty-four instead of thirty-one. But five years is long enough to get a trade properly, not just a taster. The thinking AI hits the yard office in 2031, so I'd see the writing on the wall from there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in the first year, probably electrical, because every building needs wiring and robots doing that in old houses seems a long way off. I'd use a chatbot to help with the theory, the maths bits I've forgotten. I'd keep driving full time and keep the deposit savings ticking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but with a plan it's more of a hum than a tight chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical rather than the scaffolding you mentioned before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd grab whatever I could start quickest. With five, I'd go for the one that pays better and lasts. An electrician fitting sockets in a hundred-year-old house is doing a puzzle every time, and that seems harder for a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the evening course cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two thousand over a couple of years, and two evenings a week. That's most of a year's deposit savings, so Ana and I would have to agree the house waits. I think she'd say yes, she's always told me I'm wasted in a cab.

say: I'd say five years is enough to build a **training scheme**.
I'd do **less shouting** and more organising online.
think: The driving still ends, but at **thirty-four** instead of thirty-one.
Five years is long enough to learn a **real trade**.
do: Start an **evening electrical course** in the first year.
Use a **chatbot** to help with the maths and theory.
feel: **Anxious**, but with a plan it hums rather than tightens.
S3.quote: An electrician fitting sockets in a hundred-year-old house is doing a puzzle every time, and that seems harder for a robot.
fieldNote: More time shifts him from the **quickest exit** to the best-paying one.
He'd spend about **two thousand** and delay the house.
His partner's belief that he's **wasted in a cab** quietly matters to him.

steps.text: Enrol on a two-evening-a-week electrical course
Use a chatbot to revise the course maths
Keep driving the crane truck full time while studying
Agree with Ana to delay the house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it, and I'd push the union to get training into the agreement now. Online I'd probably share the stuff about which jobs last. I'd be telling the younger lads in the yard not to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, at thirty-nine I'd still have a long working life ahead, so I'd rather move once and properly. The thinking side of the yard goes in 2036, the trucks in 2039. That's long enough to qualify, get experience, and have a trade before the robots are any good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrical course over three years instead of two, so the house can still happen. We'd buy a small place in the next few years while I'm on a driver's wage. I'd keep driving and keep the crane ticket up to date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly fine, because I'd be ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy a house. Isn't that a risk if your driving ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but Ana's wage is solid and by then I'd have a trade. And honestly we can't put our lives on hold for ten years over a maybe. I'd rather pay a mortgage than a landlord whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger lads in the yard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a second ticket while the firm still pays for training. Crane, forklift, electrical, anything. A driver with two skills sleeps better than a driver with one.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** that shouldn't be wasted.
I'd tell the **younger lads** in the yard not to panic.
think: At thirty-nine I'd still have **decades of work**, so I'd move once.
Ten years is long enough to **qualify** before robots get good.
do: Spread the **electrical course** over three years.
Buy a **small house** in the next few years on a driver's wage.
Keep the **crane ticket** current while driving.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly fine, because he'd be ahead of it.
S4.quote: A driver with two skills sleeps better than a driver with one.
fieldNote: With a decade he keeps **life plans** like the house on track.
He leans on his partner's **steady nursing wage** as a backstop.
His advice to others is practical: **get a second ticket**.

steps.text: Take the electrical qualification slowly over three years
Buy a small house with Ana within a few years
Keep the loader crane ticket up to date

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to learn a trade properly and I'd be grabbing whatever's nearest. What would help is the firm and the government paying for training while I'm still on the wage, before the office goes and the schedule gets squeezed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like for couples. My girlfriend Ana and I always assumed I'd carry the money and she'd carry the vocation. These pictures flip that. I think a lot of blokes my age would struggle with it more than they'd admit.

headlineQuote: My girlfriend Ana and I always assumed I'd carry the money and she'd carry the vocation. These pictures flip that.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old** builders' merchant driver who works a loader crane and rents with his nurse girlfriend.
He's in the **union**, uses a chatbot now and then, and learns new tools to argue with them.
He stays **calm** in the hype picture and **uneasy** when office work shifts.
In the AGI pictures he moves toward an **electrical trade**, faster or slower depending on warning time.
He quietly expects to **lean on Ana's wage**, which unsettles his sense of himself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there is no time to learn a trade properly.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** from the firm and government while he is still earning a driver's wage.
